analysis.one_liner: Lets businesses deduct the full cost of new equipment immediately, permanently.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in July 2015 and never received a vote or a hearing before the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the tax code so businesses can deduct 100 percent of the cost of qualifying equipment and property—machinery, computers, aircraft, vehicles—in the year they buy it, instead of spreading the deduction over several years. It would make this 'bonus depreciation' permanently generous, rather than letting it phase down. This lowers taxes for companies that buy expensive equipment; the cost is less federal revenue, which is made up later by other taxpayers or borrowing.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that buy large amounts of equipment—manufacturers, airlines, trucking and equipment fleets, and other capital-intensive firms—get a bigger, faster tax deduction, which reduces their tax bills in the year of purchase. Higher-income owners and investors in these businesses capture most of the benefit, since only profitable firms with large capital purchases can use the deduction. Equipment sellers can also benefit if the deduction encourages more buying.

how_it_helps.text: Increases bonus depreciation from 50% to 100% of the cost of qualifying property, letting businesses deduct the entire purchase price in year one rather than over the property's recovery period.
Makes the 100% allowance permanent by rewriting the scheduled phase-down, and applies it to property placed in service after December 31, 2014.
Allows the deduction in computing alternative minimum taxable income, so the benefit is not limited by the minimum tax.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, through reduced government revenue. A permanent immediate-expensing allowance for equipment would cost tens of billions of dollars a year in forgone federal revenue, made up by borrowing or future taxes. Businesses with little or no profit, and workers whose taxes fund the difference, get nothing from the deduction.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not include any revenue offset, so its full cost would add to federal deficits; the CRS summary and bill text show a pure tax cut with no pay-for.

The largest deductions go to the most profitable companies making the largest capital purchases; small or unprofitable businesses that cannot use the deduction get little or nothing, so the benefit is concentrated among larger firms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core policy—faster depreciation—is a real and widely used stimulus for business investment, and making the rules permanent does give companies certainty. But the version here is a pure, unoffset tax cut: the revenue cost lands on the general public, while the benefit flows overwhelmingly to profitable capital-intensive firms and their owners. A supporter would argue it pays for itself through growth; budget analysts have generally found expensing provisions do not come close to covering their revenue cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee in July 2015, and the committee never took it up—it got no markup, no vote, and never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Roger Williams introduced the Fixed Asset Relief Act of 2015 on July 23, 2015, with one Republican cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the day it was introduced.
The committee took no further action; the bill's complete action history ends with the referral, and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one changed position: the bill simply died in committee. Capital-intensive businesses neither gained the permanent 100% allowance this bill offered nor lost anything, and taxpayers avoided the unoffset revenue cost it would have carried.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers avoided an unoffset tax cut; nothing changed

for.name: Roger Williams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after its referral—no markup, no vote, and it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only support on the record was from two Republicans (the sponsor and one cosponsor), and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan opposition pattern is visible.

industries.industry: Capital-intensive corporations (manufacturers, airlines, freight and equipment fleets)
industries.note: The bill would let these firms write off 100% of equipment costs immediately, cutting their federal tax bills, with no revenue offset—so ordinary taxpayers bear the cost of the revenue loss.

Immediate expensing lowers the after-tax cost of new equipment, which can boost sales of machinery, vehicles, and aircraft; the bill includes special rules on sale-leasebacks and syndication that touch leasing structures directly.
